parts.title: My first week on a film set
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Last summer, my uncle, who works as a sound engineer, found me a job as a runner on a film set. A runner does small jobs for everybody: carrying equipment, bringing coffee and passing messages. I was excited, although I had no idea what to expect.

On the first morning, I arrived at six o'clock, but the crew had already been there for an hour. I was given a radio and told to stay close to the director's assistant, a tall woman called Greta. 'Listen carefully,' she said, 'and never be late.' Within ten minutes, she had sent me to look for a missing hat.

I soon learned that filming is mostly waiting. A scene that lasts one minute on the screen can take five hours to film, because the camera and the lights must be moved again and again. I was also surprised how often the actors repeated the same line. At first, I found this boring, but then I noticed small differences in each version, and I began to enjoy comparing them.

By Friday, I was tired but happy. Greta said that I had worked hard and asked if I would like to come back next summer. I said yes at once, although I might look for a job with more sleep.

questions.prompt: How did the writer get the job?
questions.explanation: His uncle, a sound engineer, found him the job.

questions.prompt: What did Greta tell the writer?
options: To listen and to be on time
To stay away from the actors
To wear a hat on the set
questions.explanation: She said, "Listen carefully, and never be late."

questions.prompt: What did the writer learn about filming?
questions.explanation: He says filming is mostly waiting, and a one-minute scene can take five hours.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer begin to enjoy the repeated lines?
options: He wanted to learn the words
He saw small differences each time
questions.explanation: He noticed small differences in each version and enjoyed comparing them.

questions.prompt: How does the writer feel at the end of the week?
questions.explanation: He is tired but happy and says yes at once to returning next summer.

parts.title: Our school film festival
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
Every year in March, our school holds a film festival, and this year I decided to enter a short film. [1] My friend Pia had a good idea about a boy who finds an old camera in the attic, so we wrote the story together.

We filmed during the Easter holidays, mostly in my grandmother's house. [2] That was a problem, because we needed bright light for the attic scenes. In the end, we borrowed two big lamps from the drama teacher.

The editing took much longer than we expected. [3] Pia is good with computers, so she did most of this, while I chose the music. [4] We were so nervous that we could hardly watch.

Our film did not win the first prize, but the judges gave it a special mention for its story. [5] We are already planning next year's film, and this time we want to make a comedy.
sentences: On the day of the festival, our film was shown to two hundred people.
I knew that I could not make a film alone.
It rained almost every day, so the house was very dark.
We had to cut an hour of filming down to eight minutes.
Making it taught us how much teamwork a film needs.
Pia wants to be an actor when she leaves school.

gaps.explanation: "I could not make a film alone" leads to "My friend Pia", who helps with the idea.
"That was a problem" refers to the dark house, which made bright light difficult.
"Most of this" refers to cutting the film, which is the editing.
The nervous audience scene follows the film being shown to two hundred people.
The sentence about teamwork sums up the experience before the plans for next year.

parts.title: A trip to the cinema
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage: Last Saturday, my brother and I went to the cinema to see a new adventure film. We [1] the tickets online the day before, so we did not have to wait in a queue. The film started at four o'clock, [2] we had time for a snack first. Inside, the screen was enormous, and the seats were [3] comfortable than the ones in our old cinema. The story was exciting, and I [4] never guess the ending. After the film, we talked about it [5] an hour on the bus home. My brother has asked me to go again next weekend, [6] I might have to say no because I have a lot of homework.

questions.prompt: Gap 1
questions.explanation: The action is finished and in the past, so the past simple "bought" is needed.

questions.prompt: Gap 2
questions.explanation: The film started later, so they had time: "so" shows the result.

questions.prompt: Gap 3
questions.explanation: "More comfortable than" is the comparative form used before "than".

questions.prompt: Gap 4
questions.explanation: The story is in the past, so "could never guess" fits.

questions.prompt: Gap 5
questions.explanation: "For" is used with a length of time such as an hour.

questions.prompt: Gap 6
questions.explanation: "But" shows the contrast between the invitation and the homework.

parts.title: Welcome to the Film Club
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Welcome to the Film Club! We meet in Room 5 [1] Thursdays after lessons. Anyone [2] likes making films can join. You do not need your own camera, [3] we have three that you can borrow. In the first term, we will learn [4] to use a camera and how to write a script. There is no fee, but you [5] to tell your teacher if you want to come. At the end of the year, we will show our films [6] the whole school.

gaps.explanation: We say "on" with days of the week.
A relative word for people is needed after "Anyone".
The reason for not needing a camera is that the club has some.
"How to use a camera" matches "how to write a script".
"Need to" or "have to" is followed by "tell".

parts.title: A tour of a film studio
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note with one word.

turns.speaker: marguerite
turns.text: Good afternoon, and welcome to the Hartwell Film Studio tour. I'm Marguerite, and I'll be your guide today. The tour lasts ninety minutes, so please stay together. First, we'll visit the costume room, where you can try on old clothes from famous films. Then we'll walk to the sound studio, where you'll learn how to make the noise of rain by shaking a bag of rice. After that, there's a short break at the café, where a piece of cake costs two pounds. In the last part, you'll see the model city that was built for a space film. It took six months to make. You can take photos everywhere except in the sound studio, because the equipment is very delicate. Tickets for next month's tour can be booked online. I hope you enjoy your visit.

gaps.explanation: The guide says the tour lasts ninety minutes.

gaps.prompt: In the first room, visitors try on old ___
gaps.explanation: In the costume room visitors try on old clothes from famous films.

gaps.prompt: Rice in a bag makes the noise of ___
gaps.explanation: She explains how to make the noise of rain with a bag of rice.

gaps.prompt: A piece of cake costs ___ pounds
gaps.explanation: Cake at the café costs two pounds.

gaps.prompt: The model city took ___ months to make
gaps.explanation: It took six months to make the model city.

gaps.prompt: Photos are not allowed in the ___ studio
gaps.explanation: You can take photos everywhere except in the sound studio.

parts.title: A stunt performer
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: philippa
turns.text: Today I'm talking to Jarrah Quill, who works as a stunt performer in films. Jarrah, what exactly do you do?

turns.speaker: jarrah
turns.text: I do the dangerous things that actors can't or shouldn't do, like jumping from a moving train or falling off a roof. I always train for weeks before a big scene.

turns.speaker: philippa
turns.text: Did you always want this job?

turns.speaker: jarrah
turns.text: Not at all. I was a gymnast, but I hurt my knee when I was nineteen and had to stop. A friend told me that film crews needed people who could move well, so I applied.

turns.speaker: philippa
turns.text: Is it as dangerous as it looks?

turns.speaker: jarrah
turns.text: Honestly, no. Safety is the most important thing on set. There are mats, ropes and a doctor nearby, and we practise each move slowly many times before we film it.

turns.speaker: philippa
turns.text: What is the best part of the job?

turns.speaker: jarrah
turns.text: Seeing the finished film with my family. They never know which parts are me, so I whisper, 'That was me,' and they laugh.

turns.speaker: philippa
turns.text: Do you have any advice for young people?

turns.speaker: jarrah
turns.text: Learn a sport really well and look after your body. Directors like people who are calm and patient, not only brave.

turns.speaker: philippa
turns.text: And what's next for you?

turns.speaker: jarrah
turns.text: I'm going to Canada in March to work on a film about a mountain rescue.

He takes the place of actors in dangerous scenes

questions.explanation: He does the dangerous things that actors cannot or should not do.

questions.explanation: He hurt his knee at nineteen and had to stop.
